title.en: The Young Man Carried Off by the Lion

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Young Man of the Ancient Race, who was carried off by a Lion, when asleep in the Field'

summary.en: A drowsy young hunter is picked up sleeping by a lion and wedged, alive, head-first into a zwart-storm tree; the lion licks his tears and waits to drink before eating. The man escapes in zigzags, is rolled in hartebeest skins, and the lion — a 'sorcerer' that arrows cannot kill — will take only him; at last his mother gives him up, and lion and man die together.
summary.zh: 獵者午睡，獅啣之，活嵌於樹；獅舐其淚，待飲水後再食。少年逃歸，裹以麋羚皮；獅如巫者，箭不能殺，唯欲其人。母終予之；獅與人偕死。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San legend dictated by Dia!kwain to Bleek and Lloyd, 1875; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: And he lay down on account of it; and he slept, while a lion came; it went to the water, because the noonday heat had killed it; it was thirsty; and it espied the man lying asleep; and it took up the man. And the man awoke startled... And he thought that he would not stir; for the lion would biting kill him, if he stirred... for the lion appeared to think that he was dead.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 176 (public domain).

passages.text: And the lion carried him to a zwart-storm tree; and the lion laid him in it... And it trod, pressing in the man's head between the stems of the zwart-storm tree... And it licked the man's eyes' tears. And the man wept; hence it licked the man's eyes.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 177 (public domain).

passages.text: He did not run straight; but ran first in one direction, then sprang to another place, then ran again... he called out to the people at home about it, that he had just been 'lifted up' while the sun stood high... therefore, they must look out many hartebeest-skins, that they might roll him up in them; for, he had just been 'lifted up'... And the people did so.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 183-185 (public domain); minor elisions.

passages.text: 'Ye must give a girl to the lion, that we may see whether the lion will not eat her, that it may go away.' The lion did not want the girl; for, the lion only wanted the man whom it had carried off... And the young man's mother spoke, she said: 'Ye may give my child to the lion; ye shall not allow the lion to eat my child; that the lion may go walking about; for, ye shall killing lay it upon my child; that it may die, like my child.'... And the lion bit the young man to death... And it died, while the man also lay dead.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 190-191 (public domain), minor elisions.

title.en: A Woman of the Early Race and the Rain Bull
title.zh: 早期之民女子與雨公牛

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1878 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'A Woman of the Early Race and the Rain Bull'

summary.en: The Rain bull, breathing mist, courts a woman at her hut; she throws buchu on his forehead, ties her child safe, and mounts him. She anoints him again at a great tree, and while he sleeps she climbs down and slips home, burning buchu to take the rain-scent from herself. He wakes and sinks into his spring — which, the people say, dries whenever the Rain goes out.
summary.zh: 雨公牛呼吸成霧，至屋前求愛；女子以布庫草擲其額，縛幼兒於褥，跨騎而去。至大樹再以布庫擦其頸，趁其睡爬下潛歸，焚草除雨香。牛醒，沉入其泉——凡雨出，泉必涸。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1878; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: The Rain formerly courted a young woman, while the young woman was in (her) hut, because she felt that she was still ill. The Rain scented her, and the Rain went forth, on account of it; while the place became misty... He in this manner trotting came; while the young woman was lying down, while she held (her) child on the kaross.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 193 (public domain).

passages.text: The young woman took up buchu in her hand, the young woman threw buchu upon his forehead. And she arose; and she pressed (the buchu) down upon his forehead... she pushed him away; and she took up her kaross; she tied it on. The young woman took up the child, she held the child very nicely... she laid the child down upon a kaross... She mounted the Rain; and the Rain took her away.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 194-195 (public domain), minor elisions.

passages.text: And the young woman said: 'Thou must go underneath, close to the stem of the tree.' Therefore, he went underneath, close to the stem of the tree... the young woman took out buchu, she rubbed him. Then the Rain went to sleep, on account of it. Therefore, when she saw that the Rain slept, she climbed up, she stole softly away... And she descended at a distance.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 196-197 (public domain).

passages.text: While the Rain awoke behind her back, when the Rain felt that the place was becoming cool. He arose, he walked away; he went away to the middle of the spring from which he had courting gone out, while he believed that the young woman was still sitting upon his back. He went away to the water. He went into it... she went to burn buchu... taking away the smell of the bush from herself.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 197-198 (public domain), minor elisions.

title.en: The Girl's Story; the Frogs' Story

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1874 by !Kweiten ta //Ken (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Girl's Story; the Frogs' Story'; W. H. I. Bleek, A Brief Account (1875), §41

summary.en: A girl, refusing her mothers' food, kills and eats the Water's beautiful children — striped like a zebra. A whirlwind carries her whole family, mats and all, into the spring; the girl enters first and becomes a frog, and her people become frogs after her. Their arrows and mats still grow out by the springs of the First People's land.
summary.zh: 少女不食母所予之糧，殺食水之美童——其身如斑馬紋。旋風攜其全家連褥入泉；少女先入而化為蛙，其眾亦繼化蛙。其箭與褥至今自泉中長出——此乃早期之民之地。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by !Kweiten ta //Ken to Bleek and Lloyd, 1874; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: A girl formerly lay ill; she was lying down. She did not eat the food which her mothers gave her. She lay ill. She killed the children of the Water; they were what she ate. Her mothers did not know that she did thus... [The Water was as large as a bull, and the Water's children were the size of calves, being the children of great things; beautiful, and striped like a zebra.]
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 199 with editor's note (public domain).

passages.text: And when she was seeking about for food, the clouds came up. And she spoke, she said: 'Something is not right at home; for a whirlwind is bringing (things) to the spring. For something is not going on well at home. Therefore, the whirlwind is taking (things) away to the spring.' Because her daughter killed the Water's children, therefore the whirlwind took them away to the spring.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 200-202 (public domain), minor elisions.

passages.text: The girl was the one who first went into the spring, and then she became a frog. Her mothers afterwards went into the spring; the whirlwind brought them to it... Meanwhile their daughter was in the spring; she was a frog. Her father also came to become a frog; for the whirlwind brought her father — when he was yonder on the hunting ground — to the spring.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 202-203 (public domain).

passages.text: Her father's arrows altogether grew out by the spring; for the great whirlwind had brought them to the spring. He also altogether became a frog... The mats grew out by the spring, like the arrows; their things grew out by the spring... because they were frogs.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 203-204 (public domain).

title.en: The Man Who Ordered His Wife to Cut Off His Ears

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1878 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Man who ordered his Wife to cut off his Ears'

summary.en: Thinking his younger brother's head has been skinned — when only shaved — a man of the early race insists his wife cut off his ears. She protests, he screams over his own skin, and the narrators conclude that the early race did foolish things because they were men of a different sort.
summary.zh: 早期之民誤以弟之首皮被剝（實僅剃髮），強令妻割其雙耳。妻拒之不果；己嚎己痛。敘者曰：早期之民行愚事，因其本異類。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1878; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: He formerly wished (his) wife to cut off his ears, for his younger brother's head had surely been skinned; whereas his younger brother's wife had only shaved his younger brother's head. Therefore, (his) wife cut away his ears; although (his) wife had said that she would not do so; he was the one who insisted upon it.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 205 (public domain).

passages.text: Therefore, his wife cut off his ears; and he was screaming, on account of his skin, while he himself had been the one who wished the wife to do so; for his younger brother's head had surely been skinned; whereas his younger brother had merely had his head shaved; while his wife shaved, removing the old hair.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 205 (public domain).

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1879 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The +nerru and her Husband'

summary.en: A man of the early race marries a +nerru (now a bird). She will not put earthy Bushman-rice into the kaross on her back; he snatches it, and her entrails pour out. She rises singing the house-song of the +nerru, her mother binds her up, and the husband is sent back to his own people — for they did not understand.
summary.zh: 早期之民娶內魯（今之鳥）。她不肯將帶土之米置入背之皮衣；夫強奪，其腸盡出。她起而歌內魯家族之歌；母為之縛裹；夫被遣回本族——因彼此不解。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1879; contains graphic injury; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: A man of the early race formerly married a +nerru. The +nerru put the dusty (earthy) Bushman rice into a bag, when her husband had dug out Bushman rice... He again dug out other Bushman rice. He put it in above, put in the Bushman rice on the top of the morning's Bushman rice.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 207-208 (public domain).

passages.text: And he exclaimed: 'Give me thy little kaross, that I may put the Bushman rice upon it.' And the wife said: 'We are not accustomed to put Bushman rice, having earth with it, into our back's kaross, we who are of the house of +nerru.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 209 (public domain).

passages.text: The wife's entrails, which were upon the little kaross, poured down. And he, crying, exclaimed: 'Oh dear! O my wife! What shall I do?' while the wife arose, the wife said (i.e. sang) — 'We, who are of the house of +nerru, We are not used to put earthy Bushman rice (Into) our back's kaross' — while she walked on replacing her entrails.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 210 (public domain).

passages.text: Then she ran to meet her daughter; she went to put the little kaross upon her daughter; she, holding, put her daughter's entrails upon the little kaross; and she bound up her daughter; and she slowly conducted her daughter home... Therefore, her daughter's husband went back to his own people... for, they did not understand.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 212-213 (public domain), minor elisions.

title.en: The Death of the Lizard: The Mountains That Bit Him

region.en: Strontbergen, Cape Colony (Northern Cape, South Africa)
region.zh: 南非北開普省斯特龍特山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1878 by /Han≠kass'o (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Death of the Lizard'

summary.en: The lizard, once a man of the early race, sings a marching song as he goes to live by the red sand-hills; he tries to spring through the mountain pass, and the two mountains close and bite him in two. His forepart becomes \guru-\na, his hinder part \xe-\khwai — two agama lizards — and the passes near !khau-\ka\ka bear his name.
summary.zh: 蜥蜴本為早期之人，歌行赴紅沙丘而居；欲躍過山隘，二山相合咬之為兩段。前段化為古魯那，後段化為舍夸伊——即今兩種鬣蜥。附近山隘仍以其名。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by /Han≠kass'o to Bleek and Lloyd, 1878; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: The Lizard formerly sang — 'For, I therefore intend to go, Passing through, \guru-\na's pass. And, I therefore intend to go, Passing through, \xe-\khwai's pass.' And, when he was passing through, the mountains squeezing broke him, when he had intended to pass through.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 215 (public domain).

passages.text: He seems to have thought that he would spring through the mountain pass... Then, the mountains caught him thus, the mountains bit, breaking him. Therefore, his forepart fell over and stood still, it became \guru-\na; while his hinder part fell over and stood still; it was that which became \xe-\khwai.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 215-216 (public domain).

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the narrator's remarks: he seems to have been going to the red sand hills, to dwell at them; he was going towards the pool \kau-\ka\ka, ascending along the hillside, descending into \na-\kua-rra; the place where he broke in two was where he was going to dwell.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 216-217; not verbatim.

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1876 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Baboons and ||xabbiten-||xabbiten'

summary.en: Carrying flour from the white people, ||xabbiten mocks the baboons' 'foreheads like overhanging cliffs'; they plan to beat him, and the children ask for his big head to play with. He climbs a krieboom and bluffs that the white men are coming to drive them off; the baboons flee, and he drops from the tree and runs.
summary.zh: 斑點頭自白人處背麵粉歸，譏狒狒「額如懸崖」；狒狒謀擊之，其子求其大頭為球。他攀克裏布姆樹，詐稱白人將驅之；狒狒奔逃，他自樹落下而遁。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by Dia!kwain (who heard it from ||xabbiten himself) to Bleek and Lloyd, 1876; presented as an archival record.

passages.text: The baboons espied ||xabbiten-||xabbiten, as he was coming away from the white men whom he had been to visit. He was carrying flour, which the white men gave him. And the baboons said: 'Uncle ||xabbiten-||xabbiten seems to be returning yonder; let us cross his path, that we may knock him down.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 255 (public domain).

passages.text: And ||xabbiten-||xabbiten remarked upon their foreheads' steepness. ['Ye speak to me! ye are ugly! your foreheads resemble overhanging cliffs!'] And the baboons angrily came down to ||xabbiten-||xabbiten; they broke off sticks, with which they intended to come to beat him... The baboons' children also came; going along, they called out: 'O fathers! ye must give us ||xabbiten-||xabbiten's head, that we may play with it.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 255-257 (public domain), minor elisions.

passages.text: He thought: 'I will climb a krieboom, that I may sit above in the krieboom; the baboons will have to drag me down...' And ||xabbiten-||xabbiten called out, while he deceived them, he said: 'O white men! the baboons are here, they are with me, ye must drive them away.' And the baboons ran, leaving ||xabbiten-||xabbiten; and he escaped... he quickly descended from the krieboom.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 258-259 (public domain), minor elisions.

title.en: The Child Who Set the Lion on Fire

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by !Kweiten ta //Ken (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'A Lion's Story'

summary.en: A crying child, left while her parents sleep, draws out the grass under the lion that has come for her family and sets his hair alight; he bolts and the veld burns behind him. Her mother gives her Bushman-rice, saying: hadst thou not fired the lion, we should have died — and breaks an ostrich eggshell of rice for her.
summary.zh: 啼哭之童趁獅近身，抽其身下之草，燃其鬣毛；獅遁，野火隨之。母贈桑人之米，曰：爾若不縱火，吾等必死——並為之破蛋殼盛米。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by !Kweiten ta //Ken to Bleek and Lloyd, 1875; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: The child cried there for 'Bushman rice'; a lion hearing came to her, while she cried there; her parents lay asleep... And the lion heard, as she cried there. And the lion came to her, on account of it. And she took out (some of) the grass upon which her parents were lying; because she had perceived the lion; the lion intended to kill and carry off her parents; she set the lion on fire with it.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 259-260 (public domain).

passages.text: The lion ran away; the bushes took fire. Because the child had set the lion on fire. And the child's mother afterwards gave her 'Bushman rice' because she felt that the lion would have killed them, if the child had not set the lion on fire with grass. And the lion went to die on account of the fire. Because the fire had burned, killing it.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 260 (public domain).

passages.text: And the child's mother said: 'Yes, my child, hadst thou not in this manner set the lion on fire we should have died. For thou didst set the lion on fire for us... Therefore it is, that we will break for thee an ostrich eggshell of Bushman rice; for, thou hast made us to live; we should have been dead, we should have died, hadst thou not set the lion on fire for us.'
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 260-261 (public domain).

title.en: The Man Who Found a Lion in a Cave

region.en: Katkop Mountains north of Calvinia, Northern Cape (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 南非北開普省卡茲科普山（象徵定位）

texts.period: Bushman (|Xam San) oral tradition; recorded 1875 by Dia!kwain (Bleek & Lloyd)

source.work: Bleek & Lloyd, Specimens of Bushman Folklore (1911), 'The Man who found a Lion in a Cave'

summary.en: A lion makes rain to blind a traveller, then waits asleep in a cave; the man feels the hairy thing, tiptoes out, runs to a distant fire whose flames he first takes for the lion's eyes, and survives. The lion tracks him to the people's huts, asking 'where is the man who came to me?' — and leaves when the sun rises.
summary.zh: 獅降雨蔽途，先眠穴中待之；男子觸其毛茸，踮足而出，誤認獅目為遠火，得至人群。獅循跡至屋，索問「來我處之人何在」；日出乃去。

sensitivity.note: |Xam San oral tradition dictated by Dia!kwain to Bleek and Lloyd, 1875; presented as an archival record of 19th-century colonial recordings.

passages.text: A man long ago did thus: when the rain fell he thought that he would go and sleep in a cave; when a lion had been the one who had made rain for him, so that he should not know the place at which his home seemed to be... The place was not a little dark, for, he continued to go into the bushes; he did not see the place along which he was walking.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 260-262 (public domain).

passages.text: And the lion had come first to the cave; it came to wait for the man in the cave... it fell fast asleep. And the man came, while it sat asleep. And the man, when he had entered the cave, heard a thing which seemed to breathe... he felt about; and he felt that a thing which seemed to have hair was there... he felt that a lion was the one which slept sitting inside the cave. And he gently stepped backwards and turned round; and he went out on tiptoe.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 263-264 (public domain), minor elisions.

passages.text: He espied the fire of some other people, which they kindled to warm themselves. And he thought: 'I will run to the fire which stands yonder... Didst thou not think that our fathers also said to me, that the lion's eye can also sometimes resemble a fire by night? I will look whether it be a real fire which burns there.' And he ran nearer to the fire... he saw that people were lying round in front of the fire.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), pp. 267-268 (public domain), minor elisions.

passages.text: Day broke, while the lion was still threatening them... then it was, that the lion went away, leaving the people; because the sun was rising... for the lion is a thing which is not willing to come to us, when the sun stands in the sky.
passages.note: Quote from Specimens of Bushman Folklore (Bleek & Lloyd 1911), p. 269 (public domain).
